title: Electric Circuits
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Electric Circuits Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Investigate the transfer and transformation of energy in electrical circuits, including the role of circuit components, insulators and conductors (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on electric circuits: complete loops, switches, circuit symbols and diagrams, series and parallel lamps, and finding faults. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Cells push energy around a closed circuit; a gap stops the flow.
body_html:
How to think about it

Electricity flows only around a complete loop from the cell and back.

  • A switch opens or closes a gap. Closed switch: the circuit is complete.
  • Circuit diagrams use symbols for cells, lamps, switches, buzzers and motors.
  • Series: one loop, so if one lamp blows, all go out. Parallel: separate branches, so the others stay lit.
Example

A lamp and a cell are joined with one wire. Will it light?

there is no path back to the cell

Answer: no

Example

Two lamps in parallel; one blows. The other?

its branch is still complete

Answer: stays lit

Common mistakes

  • Thinking one wire is enough (the loop must return to the cell).
  • Thinking a closed switch turns the circuit off.
  • Thinking all lamps go out when one blows in a parallel circuit.

faq.a: A complete circuit is an unbroken loop that goes from one end of the cell, through the components, and back to the other end of the cell.

faq.q: What is the difference between series and parallel circuits?
faq.a: In a series circuit everything is in one loop. In a parallel circuit there are separate branches, so each lamp can work on its own.

faq.q: Why must children not experiment with mains electricity?
faq.a: Mains electricity in Australia is 230 volts. It can cause serious burns or death. Classroom circuits use 1.5 V cells.

items.q: What does a battery do in a circuit?
c: It is the energy source that pushes current around the circuit.
It uses up all the current.
items.e: The battery stores energy and pushes the current.

items.q: Why do scientists draw circuit diagrams with symbols?
c: so anyone can understand the circuit quickly and clearly
items.e: The symbols are the same around the world.

items.q: Which carries energy from a battery to a bulb?
c: an electric current in the wires
items.e: Electric current carries the energy.

items.q: What is an electric circuit?
c: a complete path that electric current can flow around
items.e: Current flows from the battery, through the parts and back to the battery.

items.q: Two lamps are in a single loop (series). One blows. What happens to the other?
items.e: The loop is broken.

items.q: What happens to a lamp when a second cell is added in series?
items.e: More cells push more energy through the lamp.

items.q: Mia draws this circuit. Will the motor spin?
c: Yes, the loop is complete and the switch is closed.
No, there is a gap in the wire.
No, the switch is open so there is a gap.
No, there is no cell to push the current.
items.e: A component works only in a complete loop with a cell and no gaps.

items.q: Will the bulb light?
c: Yes. The circuit is closed, so current flows all the way around.
items.e: The path goes from the battery, through the bulb and back with no gaps.

items.q: Why do batteries stop working after some time?
c: The chemicals inside are used up.
items.e: Used batteries should be recycled.

items.q: In this circuit, will the motor spin?
c: No. The switch is open, so there is a gap in the path.
items.e: An open switch breaks the path. Current cannot flow.

items.q: Will the bulb light?
c: No. The switch is open, so there is a gap in the path.
items.e: An open switch breaks the path. Current cannot flow.

items.q: Will the motor spin?
c: Yes, but only for a second.
Yes. Most of the wires are connected.
No. A wire is not connected, so the circuit is open.
items.e: Every part of the loop must be connected for current to flow.

items.q: What does a switch do in a circuit?
c: It opens or closes the circuit.
items.e: A closed switch lets current flow.

No, there is a gap in the wire.

Yes, but only for a second.
Yes. Most of the wires are connected.
items.e: Every part of the loop must be connected for current to flow.

c: Yes, the loop is complete and the switch is closed.
No, there is no cell to push the current.

No, there is a gap in the wire.
items.e: A component works only in a complete loop with a cell and no gaps.

items.q: Why are the lights in a house wired in parallel?
c: so all lights go out together
so each light can be switched on and off by itself
items.e: Each branch has its own switch.

c: Yes, the loop is complete and the switch is closed.

No, there is a gap in the wire.
No, there is no cell to push the current.
items.e: A component works only in a complete loop with a cell and no gaps.

items.q: A glass marble is placed across the gap. Will the motor spin?
c: Yes, because any object closes a gap.
Yes, because it completes the circuit.
No, because it is an insulator and the circuit stays open.
items.e: Current cannot flow through an insulator, so the circuit is still open.

items.q: Matilda draws this circuit. Will the buzzer buzz?
c: No, the switch is open so there is a gap.
No, there is no cell to push the current.
Yes, the loop is complete and the switch is closed.
No, there is a gap in the wire.
items.e: A component works only in a complete loop with a cell and no gaps.

items.q: A torch has a switch on its side. What does pressing it do?
c: closes the gap so the lamp lights
items.e: Switches control circuits.

items.q: In Priya's circuit, the left switch is open and the right switch is closed. Will the lamp light up?
c: Yes, one closed switch is enough.
No, two switches can never work together.
No, at least one switch is open.
items.e: With two switches in one loop, both must be closed for current to flow.

items.q: A lamp in a circuit will not light. Two cells are both facing the same way, but the lamp still will not light. One cell is very old. What is the most likely reason?
c: One cell is flat, so there is not enough voltage.
The switch is open, so current cannot flow.
Plastic is an insulator, so it blocks the current.
The old cell had run out.
items.e: Check: cells, bulb, every connection, switches and materials.

No. There is no battery to make the current flow.
No. There is a gap in the wires.
No. The open switch makes a gap, so the circuit is not closed.
items.e: Current flows only in a closed circuit with a source of electricity.

items.q: Why are wires covered in plastic?
c: Plastic is an insulator, so it stops the current reaching our hands.
items.e: Safety.

items.q: A wooden craft stick is in the gap, and the bulb does not light. What change would make it work?
c: Replace it with another plastic object.
Replace it with a metal object, like a paper clip.
items.e: A conductor in the gap closes the circuit.

items.q: In Amelia's circuit, the left switch is open and the right switch is closed. Will the buzzer buzz?
c: No, two switches can never work together.
No, at least one switch is open.
Yes, one closed switch is enough.
items.e: With two switches in one loop, both must be closed for current to flow.

items.q: A lamp in a circuit will not light. A plastic paperclip has been used to join two wires. What is the most likely reason?
c: Plastic is an insulator, so it blocks the current.
Six lamps share the voltage of one cell, so each gets very little.
The switch is open, so current cannot flow.
items.e: Check: cells, bulb, every connection, switches and materials.

c: Six lamps share the voltage of one cell, so each gets very little.
There is a gap, so the circuit is not complete.
Plastic is an insulator, so it blocks the current.
One cell is flat, so there is not enough voltage.

items.q: How can you make the buzzer buzz?

items.e: Closing the switch completes the loop.

Replace it with a metal object, like a paper clip.

Yes, one closed switch is enough.
No, at least one switch is open.
items.e: With two switches in one loop, both must be closed for current to flow.

items.q: How can you make the motor spin?
c: Wrap the wire in tape so it does not touch.
items.e: The loose wire leaves a gap. Connect it to close the circuit.

items.q: What is the difference between a cell and a battery?
c: A cell is bigger than a battery.
A battery is two or more cells joined together.
items.e: We often call one cell a battery in everyday life.

items.q: What does this circuit symbol show?
items.e: A battery (two or more cells) is drawn as two cell symbols joined together.

items.q: Which component does this symbol stand for?

items.e: Learn each symbol's shape.

items.q: What does this circuit symbol show?
items.e: A buzzer is drawn as a half circle on the wire.

items.q: In a cell symbol, which line shows the positive side?
items.e: Long line = positive (+).

items.q: Which component has a symbol that is a circle with the letter M inside?
items.e: Learn each symbol's shape.

c: as two cell symbols joined together

items.e: Learn each symbol's shape.

items.q: What does this circuit symbol show?
items.e: A lamp (bulb) is drawn as a circle with a cross inside.
A bulb in a branch with an open switch does not light. The other branches are complete circuits.

items.q: 2 identical bulbs are connected in series to a battery, as shown. One bulb blows. How many bulbs stay lit?
items.e: In series, there is only one path. When one bulb blows, the circuit is broken and all the bulbs go out.

items.q: Why does a torch need a closed switch to work?
c: The switch completes the circuit so current can flow.
items.e: An open switch leaves a gap.

items.q: 4 identical bulbs are connected in parallel to a battery, as shown. One bulb blows. How many bulbs stay lit?
items.e: In parallel, each bulb has its own path, so the others stay lit.

items.q: Why are the lights in a house connected in parallel?
c: They are cheaper to switch off together.
Each light can be switched on and off on its own, and one fused bulb does not affect the others.
items.e: Homes use parallel circuits.

items.q: A torch has two batteries in series. One battery is put in the wrong way round. What happens?
c: The bulb does not light or is very dim.
items.e: The batteries push against each other.

items.q: What happens to a lamp's brightness when more lamps are added in series with one cell?
items.e: The cell's energy is shared between more lamps.

items.q:
Circuit A
Circuit B
Circuit A has 1 battery and 2 bulbs in series. Circuit B has 2 batteries and 2 bulbs in series. All the batteries and bulbs are the same. In which circuit is each bulb brighter?
items.e: More batteries in series make bulbs brighter. Bulbs in series share and are dimmer; each bulb in parallel is as bright as one bulb alone.

items.q: 2 identical bulbs are connected in parallel to a battery, as shown. One bulb blows. How many bulbs stay lit?
items.e: In parallel, each bulb has its own path, so the others stay lit.

items.q: Which is safe for a classroom circuit investigation?
c: mains power from a wall socket
1.5 V cells, wires and small lamps
wet wires and a 230 V plug
a car battery and bare hands
items.e: Mains electricity in Australia is 230 V and can kill.

items.e: More batteries in series make bulbs brighter. Bulbs in series share and are dimmer; each bulb in parallel is as bright as one bulb alone.

items.q: Two batteries are connected in parallel to one bulb. How does the bulb compare with a bulb lit by one battery?
c: It is equally bright, but the batteries last longer.
items.e: Batteries in parallel share the work.

items.q: Two bulbs are connected in series. One bulb fuses. What happens to the other bulb?
c: It becomes dimmer but stays lit.
items.e: In series there is only one path for the current.

items.q:
Circuit A
Circuit B
Circuit A has 3 batteries and 3 bulbs in series. Circuit B has 2 batteries and 1 bulb. All the batteries and bulbs are the same. In which circuit is each bulb brighter?
items.e: More batteries in series make bulbs brighter. Bulbs in series share and are dimmer; each bulb in parallel is as bright as one bulb alone.

items.q: What is the job of a switch?
c: to open or close a gap in the circuit
items.e: A closed switch completes the loop.

items.q: What does a circuit need for a lamp to light?
c: a complete loop from the battery through the lamp and back
one wire from the battery to the lamp
items.e: Electricity flows only around a complete loop.

items.q:
Circuit A
Circuit B
Circuit A has 1 battery and 3 bulbs in series. Circuit B has 3 batteries and 3 bulbs in parallel. All the batteries and bulbs are the same. In which circuit is each bulb brighter?
items.e: More batteries in series make bulbs brighter. Bulbs in series share and are dimmer; each bulb in parallel is as bright as one bulb alone.

items.q: Two lamps are on separate branches (parallel). One blows. What happens to the other?
c: It gets dimmer and goes out.
items.e: Its own branch is still a complete loop.

items.q: This circuit has 3 bulbs. How many bulbs light up?
items.e: A bulb in a branch with an open switch does not light. The other branches are complete circuits.

items.q: Which component pushes electricity around a circuit?
items.e: The cell is the energy source.

items.q: Why should you never put metal objects into a plug socket?
c: Metal conducts electricity, so mains current could flow through you.
items.e: Safety.

items.q: Ella's buzzer makes a quiet sound. Which change would make it louder?
items.e: More energy from the cells makes the buzzer louder.

items.q: Tom tests 6 objects in a circuit tester. Which result shows an object is a conductor?
c: The bulb lights when the object is in the gap.
items.e: If current flows through it, it is a conductor.

items.q: A buzzer is quiet compared with yesterday, with the same circuit. Why?
c: Buzzers always get quieter on Tuesdays.
items.e: Voltage drops as cells run down.

items.q: Jack adds a second lamp in series and both lamps are dimmer. What could he change to make them brighter?
items.e: More cells, brighter lamps.

items.q: Why should you never use water near electrical outlets?
c: Water with impurities can conduct electricity to your body.
items.e: Tap water conducts electricity and can carry dangerous current.

items.q: How would you show a motor in a circuit diagram?
c: as a long and short line
as a circle with a cross
as a circle with the letter M inside
items.e: M for motor.

items.q: Ruby's circuit has a battery, a bulb and a buzzer in one loop. She unscrews the bulb. What happens to the buzzer?
c: It stops, because the loop is broken.
items.e: In a single loop, a break anywhere stops the current everywhere.

items.q: Which list describes the components in this circuit?
c: one cell, one motor and one open switch
two cells, one motor and one open switch
one cell, two motors and one open switch
items.e: Count each symbol. A single cell is one long line and one short line.

items.q: Why must a circuit diagram show a complete loop?
c: Current flows in straight lines only.
Current only flows around a complete circuit.
items.e: No gaps.

items.q: Which list describes the components in this circuit?
items.e: Count each symbol. A single cell is one long line and one short line.

items.q: A student draws a lamp as a plain circle. Why is this a problem?
c: Others may not know it is a lamp; the lamp symbol has a cross inside.
items.e: Use recognised symbols.

items.q: Mia adds a second battery to her circuit, and the bulb gets brighter. What does this show?
c: More energy is being delivered to the bulb.
items.e: Two batteries push more current, so more energy reaches the bulb.

items.q: Why should you never test circuits with a wall socket?
c: Mains electricity is 230 V and can cause serious injury.
Wall sockets only work at night.
items.e: Use only cells in class.

items.q: A circuit has a motor that spins a fan. What energy change happens in the motor?
c: electrical energy to energy of motion
items.e: Motors turn electrical energy into motion.

items.q: What happens to the brightness of bulbs when more bulbs are added in series?
items.e: Bulbs in series share the electrical energy.

items.q: Why do electricians in different countries understand the same diagram?
c: They all use the same recognised symbols.
items.e: International symbols.

items.q: Why does a car have a switch for each light rather than one for everything?
c: so each light can be controlled on its own
items.e: Separate control.

items.q: Ruby wants one switch to turn on two lamps at the same time. Where should the switch go?
c: in the main part of the circuit, next to the cell
items.e: A switch in the main loop controls everything.

items.q: How could you use a circuit to test whether a material conducts electricity?
c: Put the material across a gap in a lamp circuit and see if the lamp lights.
items.e: Conductor tester.
